title: Baseline Performance of AI Tools in Classifying Cognitive Demand of Mathematical Tasks
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether current artificial intelligence tools can accurately classify the cognitive demand of mathematics tasks using the Task Analysis Guide (TAG), a well-established framework from mathematics education. The authors focus on a practical question relevant to teacher planning: can AI meaningfully support teachers in judging whether a task is low- or high-demand, and can it distinguish among the four TAG categories of Memorization, Procedures without Connections, Procedures with Connections, and Doing Mathematics?

To test this, the researchers uploaded the TAG and twelve mathematics tasks to eleven AI tools, including six general-purpose systems (such as ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, and Perplexity) and five education-specific systems (including Khanmigo, Magic School, Brisk, Coteach AI, and School.AI). They used a single standardized prompt without prompt engineering to establish a baseline, and they examined both overall classification accuracy and detailed reasoning patterns when the tools made errors. The tasks were drawn from mathematics teacher-training contexts and represented all four cognitive demand levels.

The study found that AI tools were correct only about 62-63% of the time on average, with no education-specific tool clearly outperforming general-purpose tools. Performance was especially strong for Procedures without Connections tasks and much weaker for Memorization and Doing Mathematics tasks. The tools showed a strong middle-category bias, often defaulting to Procedures with or without Connections, and their explanations frequently over-weighted surface features rather than deeper cognitive requirements. The authors conclude that these tools are not yet reliable for autonomous use in task analysis, though they may be useful as decision-support tools with human oversight and improved prompting.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a clearly described empirical benchmark study, but it is not a causal impact study and does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental design. Evidence quality is limited by the small task set, single-prompt protocol, and reliance on accuracy benchmarking rather than an educational outcome trial.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests meaningful but uncertain practical value for teacher workflow support, especially given 62% average accuracy and Khanmigo’s 50% accuracy. There is no demonstrated learner impact, so the current effect on educational practice is modest and indirect.

interventions.use_case: Baseline evaluation of multiple AI tools, including Khanmigo, for classifying the cognitive demand of K-12 mathematics tasks using the Task Analysis Guide with a single standardized prompt.
Khanmigo is included as an education-specific conversational AI tool and benchmarked on its ability to analyze and classify math task cognitive demand from uploaded documents.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies whether AI tools, including Khanmigo, can reduce teacher planning workload by accurately classifying math task cognitive demand. Across 133 classifications, average accuracy was 62%, with Khanmigo at 50%, indicating limited readiness for autonomous use but some potential as a decision-support aid.
finding.measure: Accuracy of AI classification of mathematical task cognitive demand; task-level and tool-level percent correct
finding.study_size: n=133 classifications across 12 tasks and 11 AI tools

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates AI tools’ ability to classify the cognitive demand of mathematics tasks using the Task Analysis Guide. Average accuracy across tools was 62%, ranging from 9% to 100% by task; Khanmigo achieved 50% overall accuracy, suggesting substantial limitations for mathematically grounded task analysis without human oversight.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy for math task cognitive demand across four TAG categories
finding.study_size: n=12 mathematics tasks; n=11 AI tools
